questions.stem: `Ledger extends ArrayList<Long>` overrides only `add(Long)`, which throws for a negative amount. A correction routine written for any `List<Long>` is given a `Ledger` holding one entry and calls `list.set(0, -300L)`. What happens?

options.text: The call throws, since a write to a Ledger goes through the rule that the Ledger class declares
options.says: the subclass overrode add only; set is ArrayList's own method, which the rule never sees

options.text: The call throws, since ArrayList's set stores the element through add, which reaches the override
options.says: ArrayList.set replaces the element without calling add, so the override never runs and nothing checks the amount

options.text: The amount is stored, since set is inherited unchanged and knows nothing of the Ledger's rule
options.says: a subclass inherits every public method of its superclass, and callers of the superclass type may use any of them

options.text: The amount is stored, since the routine's List<Long> parameter makes the call run List's version of set
options.says: an instance method is chosen by the object's class, not the declared type; the amount is stored because ArrayList.set has no check

origin.section: A Subclass Can Be Used Wherever Its Superclass Is, So It Inherits Every Promise the Superclass Makes

questions.stem: `Sensor` declares `public String unit() { return "raw"; }`. Interface `Celsius` declares `default String unit() { return "C"; }`. `Thermometer extends Sensor implements Celsius` declares no methods. What does `Celsius t = new Thermometer(); t.unit()` return?

options.text: "C", since a call through an interface type runs that interface's default unless the class overrides it
options.says: the object's class decides; Thermometer inherits Sensor's public method, which beats the default however it is called

options.text: "C", since an interface the class names itself takes priority over a method it inherits from a superclass
options.says: a method from the class hierarchy wins over any default, however the interface is listed

options.text: "raw", since a method the class inherits from a superclass takes priority over an interface's default
options.says: class methods win; the default would run only if Thermometer overrode unit() to call Celsius.super.unit()

options.text: "raw", since the first type in the class's declaration takes priority over the types listed after it
options.says: the order of the declaration plays no part; a superclass's public method wins over a default by rule

questions.stem: Interfaces `Rechargeable` and `Networked` each declare a default `String status()`, and neither extends the other. `Device implements Rechargeable` and declares nothing else. `Phone extends Device implements Networked` declares no methods. What happens with `new Phone().status()`?

options.text: It returns Rechargeable's text, since Device passes it down as a superclass method, which beats a default
options.says: a superclass's method beats a default only when a class declares it; a default that Device inherits is still a default

options.text: It returns Networked's text, since Phone names Networked itself, which makes it the more specific one
options.says: more specific means one interface extends the other; these two are unrelated

options.text: Phone doesn't compile, since it gets status() from two defaults and has to choose between them itself
options.says: the compiler reports unrelated defaults; Phone must override status() and choose with Rechargeable.super or Networked.super

options.text: Phone compiles, and the call throws IncompatibleClassChangeError, since the JVM has to choose between them
options.says: that error appears only for class files compiled before the conflict existed; from source, the compiler refuses Phone

questions.stem: `Invoice implements Exportable, Auditable` was compiled against a library in which only `Exportable` has a default `String label()`. The next library version adds a default `String label()` to `Auditable`. The application is deployed with the new library and without being recompiled. What happens?

options.text: It starts, and label() returns Exportable's text, since which default runs was fixed when Invoice was compiled
options.says: the class file doesn't fix which default runs; the JVM looks at the interfaces it loads, and now finds two

options.text: It starts, and the first label() call throws IncompatibleClassChangeError, since the two defaults now conflict
options.says: the class loads and its other methods work; only a call to the conflicting method fails

options.text: It fails as Invoice is loaded, with IncompatibleClassChangeError, since the two defaults now conflict
options.says: the class loads and its other methods run; the error comes at the call to label()

options.text: It fails as Invoice is loaded, with a VerifyError, since its bytecode no longer matches the library
options.says: nothing in Invoice's bytecode changed or fails verification; the error comes at the call to label()
